questions.prompt: Complete with the right form of "to break out": "An ___ of flu closed three primary schools in the district."
questions.explanation: After the article "an" the sentence needs a noun, and the noun made from the phrasal verb break out is the compound "outbreak", in which the particle jumps in front of the verb — as in outcome and outlook. The -ing form, the base form and the past form are all verb forms and none of them can follow an article.

questions.prompt: Complete: "Our school club ___ its own website three weeks ago."
questions.explanation: "Three weeks ago" names a moment that is over and closed, and a closed moment takes the past simple. The present perfect refuses a finished time marker, the present simple would turn the event into a habit, and the past perfect would need a second, later past event to look back from.

questions.prompt: Match each prefix with the base word it combines with to form a real English word.
questions.explanation: The negative prefix chooses its form from the first letter of the word: "im-" before m, p and b gives impatient, and "il-" before l gives illegal. "Un-" and "dis-" obey no letter rule and are learnt word by word: unreachable and disability. The tempting mistakes are "unpatient" and "unlegal", which pick the prefix by ear instead of by spelling. Note that ability also gives inability, a real word with a different meaning — but in- is not on the board here.

questions.prompt: Complete: "___ he worked full time, he cooked the evening meal every day."
questions.explanation: "Although" opens a subordinate clause of contrast at the front of the sentence and lets it run on to the main clause after the comma. "But" joins two clauses from the middle of a sentence, not from the front; "However" needs a full stop before it and a comma right after it; and "Therefore" would announce a consequence, which is the opposite of the contrast this sentence expresses.

questions.prompt: Complete: "He has been the head of that primary school ___ 2004."
questions.explanation: "Since" introduces the point in time when the situation started; "for" would introduce its length, as in for twenty-one years; "during" needs a period seen as a whole, as in during the holidays; and "from" opens a stretch that has to be closed by to, as in from 2004 to 2011.

questions.prompt: Three of these words belong to the same lexical field. Which one does NOT?
questions.explanation: Enrolment, graduation and syllabus all belong to the field of education — registering for a course, finishing it, and the list of what it contains. "Eruption" belongs to nature, next to sandstorm and typhoon. Grouping words by field is what lets you guess the meaning of a new word from the words around it.
